Senses.Explanation: To receive someone and lead them onward. In Chan records it commonly names reception of students by named teachers and the answers given when students come before them. Asked, “how do you receive and lead?” (作麼生接引), Juelang Daosheng answers, “every house has a road open to carts and horses” (家家有路通車馬). Konggu Daocheng, asked “by which gate do you receive and lead later students?” (以那一門接引後學), answers with the recorded alternatives of staff and shout, expedient and actual, opposing and following. An unnamed questioner says, “I too hope to be received and led” (某甲亦望接引), and Konggu replies, “one cannot walk by taking another by the hand; only one's own assent is intimate” (把手牽人行不得，為人自肯乃方親). Qianshan Hanke asks whether the fundamental matter can be used to receive people, then sets “if there is receiving” against “without relying on receiving” (若有接引；不假接引). Guxue Zhe invokes the Yellow-faced Master in a hall address as having received and led in many ways (多方接引); this is retained because Guxue Zhe deploys the Zen Buddha from the teaching seat, not as evidence imported from outside the Chan records. Thus the corpus uses an ordinary verb of reception as a category for named teachers' dealings with arrivals, while also recording challenges to the category itself; it supplies no single fixed procedure under the word.

Senses.Explanation: To receive it means to take possession of a concrete item handed over in an encounter or ceremony. Linji takes a Chan board and immediately strikes; Manjusri accepts the offered sprig and displays it as medicine; Foyan Qingyuan receives a ceremonial document; Hongzhi Zhengjue receives the transmission robe. Uses for receiving a person, gaining a place, or successfully handling someone are distinct relations and are not folded into this object sense.

Senses.PreferredTarget: gruel
Senses.Explanation: Gruel (粥) is the thin cooked-grain meal served in the monastery, ordinarily the morning member of the recurring pair ‘gruel and rice’ (粥飯). The word retains that concrete referent throughout the record: the monastic code directs that opening the bowl and eating gruel or rice, tea or broth, be done carefully, and a kitchen exchange distinguishes cooking rice from cooking gruel (炊飯耶煮粥耶). Chan bends this everyday meal by repeatedly putting it into public answers and named cases. Asked for ‘talk that surpasses buddhas and patriarchs,’ Changping answers ‘eating gruel and eating rice’ (喫粥喫飯); asked about the student's own self, Guizong answers ‘when the gruel is thin, sit down later’ (粥稀後坐). In Zhaozhou's case, a newly arrived monastic asks for instruction; Zhaozhou asks, ‘have you eaten your gruel?’ (喫粥了也未), and after the questioner says yes, tells him, ‘go wash your bowl’ (洗鉢盂去). Yunmen preserves the exchange and explicitly asks whether Zhaozhou gave an instruction. Later records repeatedly quote and comment on the same question-and-answer. The meal also supplies the record's language for the ordinary allotment: Baichi says ‘eating gruel and eating rice is your own basic lot’ (喫粥喫飯是汝本分事), while a Zhaozhou saying names the two daily gruel-and-rice meals as his only occasion of ‘mixed use of mind’ (除二時粥飯是雜用心處). In the Ganzhi–Nanquan case, Ganzhi provides gruel and requests the meal recitation; Nanquan dedicates it to ‘the tabby cat and white ox’ (貍奴白牯), after which Ganzhi leaves and Nanquan breaks the cooking pot. Thus the corpus does not turn gruel into a second object or an abstract substance: it keeps the food concrete while deploying eating, serving, and washing up in answers, institutional schedules, and public cases.
Senses.Note: Zen-allowlist concordance: the headword has 2,824 hits in 341 files; eat-gruel forms have 748 in 182; gruel-and-rice forms have 668 in 223; the completed-meal question has 101 in 67; and the gruel-and-rice monastic epithet has 59 in 42. Standard definition-formula searches all returned zero. Eighteen grammatical strings meaning ‘as for gruel’ or ‘one who handles gruel’ occur in service contexts or named phrases, not definitions. Sense audit: ordinary breakfast gruel, offered or cooked gruel, and the food in Zhaozhou's case are the same thing. Related entries should keep the eating bowl separate from the robe-and-bowl succession token, and should give the gruel-and-rice monastic epithet its own lexical article rather than assigning that human referent to the standalone food word.

Senses.PreferredTarget: the monastery's meal routine
Senses.Explanation: The joined food words also name a monastery's scheduled communal meals and their provision. The Imperially Revised Baizhang Monastic Code, redacted by Dongyang Dehui, schedules gruel and rice at two times and tea and hot water at three (二時上粥飯。三時上茶湯。). Zhaozhou Congshen likewise says that, during his travels, the two scheduled gruel-and-rice meals were the only occasions that divided his attention (除二時粥飯是雜用心處). Baoning Renyong calls himself a gruel-and-rice host (粥飯主人) who receives travellers from north and south with salt, vinegar, sufficient gruel, and sufficient rice. Here the headword is not merely a list of two foods: it names recurring communal provision, its timetable, and the host responsible for it. Zen bends the ordinary food pair into the institutional vocabulary of monastery scheduling and hospitality.
Senses.Note: The allowlisted concordance has 668 hits in 223 texts. Institutional families include the two gruel-and-rice mealtimes (二時粥飯) and the gruel-and-rice host (粥飯主人). These are deployments of one communal meal system, not separate senses. That organized institution is distinct from the physical food eaten and smelled in the second sense.

Senses.PreferredTarget: gruel and cooked rice
Senses.Explanation: Gruel and cooked rice are the physical foods smelled, tasted, eaten, and shown restoring movement in Chan records. This food referent is distinct from the monastery's organized meal schedule and provision. Shiwu Qinghong says that mountain-field gruel and rice smell fragrant (山田粥飯香). Foyan Qingyuan asks whether someone unfed gruel and rice for three days can move, then says that the person can move after eating some (不與粥飯喫三日……纔方喫得些粥飯方能動得). Boshan Wuyi says that only now, when eating gruel and rice, does he know sweetness (至今喫粥飯始知甜耳). Xueyan Zuqin describes residents merely following the crowd to eat gruel and rice and perform bodily functions (趂大隊，喫粥飯，屙屎送尿). Baichi Yuan's related enumeration places eating gruel and eating rice among ordinary bodily acts, while Tiebians Yunshao's rebuke derives a longer compound from consumed food, “puffing gruel-and-rice breath” (鼓粥飯氣). Eating, taste, fragrance, and restored movement predicate physical food, a different thing from the monastery's schedule and provision.
Senses.Note: Four exact headword witnesses establish the food referent through fragrance, nourishment, taste, and consumption. Two marked family witnesses preserve the separated eating formula and the food-derived breath compound without allowing either to count toward exact-headword depth. Longer compounds such as gruel-and-rice monk remain separate lexical families.

Senses.PreferredTarget: a gruel-and-rice monk
AlternateTargets: a monk living on communal meals
Senses.Explanation: A gruel-and-rice monk is an ordinary monastery resident living within the community's daily support. Chan records use the same human role in self-description, refusal of public office, prohibition, contrast, and vow; those appraisals do not turn the resident into different kinds of person. Fenyang Shanzhao, repeatedly summoned to prestigious monasteries, says, “I am a long-term gruel-and-rice monk; transmitting the buddha-mind lineage is no small matter” (我長行粥飯僧傳佛心宗非細事也) and refuses eight invitations. Huaiyu Xuan Shouzuo declines Nanyuan by saying that he has long been a gruel-and-rice monk and will not emerge into the human world. Baoci Guangyun simply identifies himself as one. In contrastive uses, an official asks whether Weishan Lingyou's assembly consists of monks who eat gruel and rice or monks who investigate Chan; Weishan repeats and rejects both categories. Zhenjing Kewen warns the assembly not to become long-term gruel-and-rice monks. Xiangyan Zhixian says he will stop studying the buddha teaching and become one, sparing his mind the labor, while Puming's verse joins the same role to ceasing pursuit of learned knowledge yet insisting on clarifying mind. The Zen bend lies in making ordinary communal subsistence a public identity and test. Approval, self-deprecation, refusal, and rebuke are readings of one role, not separate senses.
Senses.Note: The headword has 59 hits in 42 allowlisted texts. The earlier two-sense split was rejected on independent review: institutional residence and being characterized by the meals that support it do not establish incompatible referents. The exact same long-term gruel-and-rice-monk form occurs in refusal and admonition contexts, proving that appraisal and surrounding contrast cannot define separate senses. Related food and insult terms remain lexically distinct and do not donate stronger meanings to this compound.

Collected Raising of Old Cases of the School: The commentary names Baiyan Fu and records his verdict: although the two old teachers’ exchange sounds like jade and gold, seen with the true eye it is altogether drumming gruel-and-rice breath.

Senses.Explanation: Gruel-and-rice breath is the meal-fed breath behind speech, turned in Chan records into a cutting name for verbal display that does not itself settle the matter under question. Zhaozhou Congshen gives the phrase itself when asked for the true teaching eye. The answer makes ordinary meal-fed breath occupy the place where the questioner requests an elevated principle, without converting food into a hidden substance. Elsewhere the compound is explicitly critical. Jiufeng Shao says rehearsed material brought to the hall only smokes the community with gruel-and-rice breath; Tiebian Yunshao says even seamless question-and-answer can amount to empty drumming with it. Xuetang Daoxing applies the verdict to surplus commentary on Yunmen, while Zhongfeng Mingben and Baiyan Fu use the same drumming image when judging inherited encounter performance. The repeated job is to expose impressive talk as still powered by eating and breathing. The phrase can therefore be an answer or a criticism, but those are uses of one image rather than different things. It does not mean gruel’s aroma, and it does not make ordinary meals contemptible.

Senses.Explanation: The tiny mustard seed is the records’ scale-comparison object, repeatedly paired with reversals in which Mount Sumeru is contained within it. The graphs name a mustard seed, and the term is well attested in the corpus. Its small size supplies the comparison ‘mustard-seed-sized’ (芥子許, attested 76 times across 54 source records representing 54 works), as when a named record subject speaks of a doubt as small as a mustard seed. The corpus also repeatedly pairs the seed with Mount Sumeru in both directions: ‘Sumeru contains a mustard seed’ (須彌納芥子, attested 57 times across 40 source records representing 38 works) and ‘a mustard seed contains Sumeru’ (芥子納須彌, attested 71 times across 56 source records representing 54 works). In the Guizong encounter, Li Bo accepts the first statement but asks whether the second is false; Guizong asks where Li Bo’s ten thousand books are held in a body the size of a coconut. In another exchange, the two directions receive the one-word answers ‘easy’ and ‘difficult.’ A later address records mountains, earth, trees, monastics, laypeople, sages, and ordinary people placed inside a mustard seed without the seed becoming narrow. These are the corpus’s recorded scale constructions; the entry does not turn them into a symbolic meaning for the seed.
